lesson.title: Flood the Network, Then Compute: How Link State Routing Works
lesson.summary: Link state routing has every router flood its local link costs to the entire network so each router can build a complete map and independently compute shortest paths, in contrast to distance vector routing's neighbor-only information sharing.
lesson.body:
Every router in a network needs to answer the same basic question: given where I am, what is the best next hop toward every possible destination? A routing algorithm is the general strategy for answering that question, and link state routing is one of the two dominant strategies used in real networks, the other being distance vector. The core idea behind link state routing is disarmingly simple: instead of routers trading rumors about how far things are, every router tells the whole network exactly what its own local connections look like, and then each router independently works out the rest.

Concretely, each router first discovers its directly attached neighbors and measures, or is configured with, the cost of each link to them, a cost that might reflect bandwidth, delay, or simply be set to one for basic hop counting. The router packages this information, its identity plus the list of neighbors and link costs, into a link state advertisement and floods it to every other router in the network, not just its immediate neighbors. Flooding means each router that receives a new advertisement it has not seen before forwards a copy out all of its other links, so the advertisement rapidly reaches every router in the network, each of which stores a copy. Because every router floods its own advertisement, every router ends up holding a complete, identical set of advertisements, one from each router in the network, a data structure usually called the link state database. This database is effectively a full map of the network's topology: which routers exist, which links connect them, and what each link costs.

Once a router holds this map, it does not need to ask anyone anything else. It runs a shortest path algorithm, almost always Dijkstra's algorithm, on its own copy of the topology to compute the least cost path from itself to every other router. Because every router started from the same map, every router computes a mutually consistent set of routes, and no router's view of the shortest path to a given destination depends on trusting a distance reported by someone else who might itself be wrong or out of date.

This is the sharpest contrast with distance vector routing. A distance vector router never sees the topology at all, it only ever learns, from each neighbor, that neighbor's current best distance to each destination, and then picks a next hop by adding its own link cost to the smallest of those reported distances. That works, but it means a router's knowledge is only ever secondhand and one hop deep, errors and stale information can propagate and compound, the classic count to infinity problem when a link fails, and convergence after a topology change can be slow because information has to ripple hop by hop through the whole network. Link state routing avoids this by not asking any router to trust a neighbor's summary at all, everyone gets the raw facts directly from their source and computes independently. The price is more control traffic, since every router's advertisement has to reach every other router, and more computation per router, since each one runs a shortest path algorithm over the whole topology, but the payoff is faster, more reliable convergence and a network that is much easier to reason about, since at any instant every well behaved router agrees on what the network actually looks like.
